Trustworthy Evaluation of AI-Assisted Painting Restoration

Multi-Model Comparison Report

Evaluation population: 410 paired cases from 50 paintings
Full-scope models: OpenCV Telea, LaMa, Stable Diffusion
Partial-scope model: SDXL on 10 predeclared cases
Evidence: classical, perceptual, feature, spatial, texture, colour, seam, semantic, uncertainty, and runtime
Validation status: passed through Batch 8

Research-question orientation

  • RQ1: Does multi-metric evaluation reveal behaviour that traditional similarity alone cannot?
  • RQ2: How do methods differ across damage conditions, categories, and styles?
  • RQ3: Does repeated-seed variability identify unstable or potentially speculative Stable Diffusion restorations?
  • Extended scope: Where do metrics disagree, how stable are rankings, and which cases require human review?

Executive conclusions

  • LaMa has the broadest full-scope numerical support: it leads 9 of 10 evidence-family outcomes.
  • Telea retains a distinct structural niche: it leads 1 overall family outcome and the selected thin-scratch case shows a clear deterministic advantage over Stable Diffusion.
  • Stable Diffusion does not lead an overall core family: its strengths are conditional, while thin scratches can remain visible as line-shaped artifacts.
  • Damage and evidence type materially change the answer: 63 of 79 scope groups (79.7%) contain divided family evidence.
  • Overall rankings are painting-sensitive but generally stable: the median core anchor winner survives 100.0% of leave-one-painting-out replicates.
  • Prompt engineering is not a universal fix: the scratch-aware prompt improves masked MAE in 32.0%, crop SSIM in 28.0%, and seam evidence in 42.0% of paired scratch cases.
  • SDXL remains exploratory: it leads 0 of 10 family outcomes in its bounded subset and cannot be generalized to 410 cases.
  • Generative inference carries a substantial operational cost: Stable Diffusion's core median runtime is approximately 22.5 times Telea's.
Main conclusion. The results support conditional model selection, not a universal leaderboard: LaMa is the strongest broad baseline, Telea remains valuable for constrained local geometry, and generative methods require additional scrutiny for local fidelity, stability, and unsupported content.

  • LaMa leads most overall classical, perceptual, feature, colour, seam, semantic, spatial, and texture-family evidence.
  • Telea's overall advantage is concentrated rather than universal.
  • Stable Diffusion's absence from the overall family leaders does not mean it loses every case; it means its advantages do not persist across the full paired population.
  • Metric disagreement is common enough to change interpretation and must remain visible.
RQ1 conclusion. Traditional similarity describes only part of restoration behaviour. Texture, colour, seam, feature, and semantic evidence materially alter how some candidates are interpreted.

2. How do the models differ overall?

LaMa

  • Provides the strongest broad evidence-family consistency.
  • Remains the dominant family-balanced outcome across many conditional groups.
  • Still produces visible smoothing or residual artifacts in individual cases, so numerical leadership is not equivalent to flawless restoration.

OpenCV Telea

  • Has the lowest computational cost among the evaluated methods.
  • Is particularly competitive when damage geometry permits local interpolation.
  • Shows a pronounced advantage over Stable Diffusion in the selected thin-scratch evidence.
  • Can produce blur or dark filling artifacts for less locally constrained losses.

Stable Diffusion

  • Provides condition-specific generative continuation rather than a stable global advantage.
  • Can preserve semantic or feature evidence while losing colour, seam, or local fidelity.
  • Shows repeated-seed variability and prompt sensitivity unavailable in deterministic methods.
  • Can replace a white scratch with a subtler but still visible tonal line.
Overall model conclusion. LaMa is the strongest general-purpose computational baseline in this experiment. Telea remains preferable for some narrow local repairs. Stable Diffusion presents a semantic-continuation versus local-fidelity trade-off rather than a consistent improvement.

3. What do the restorations actually look like?

Visual conclusion. The representative cases confirm that metric winners can retain visible defects and that different metrics reward different aspects of the same restoration. Numerical ranking therefore requires image-level review.

4. Does performance depend on damage geometry?

  • loss large: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.
  • loss small: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.
  • mixed damage: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.
  • not applicable: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.

  • zero control: Tie / unresolved is the family-balanced majority outcome.
  • 0%: Tie / unresolved is the family-balanced majority outcome.
  • 10%: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.
  • 11.5%: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.
  • 12.5%: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.
  • 15%: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.
  • 2%: Tie / unresolved is the family-balanced majority outcome.
  • 20%: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.
  • 4%: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.

Damage-geometry conclusion. Model behaviour changes with both damage type and damaged-area fraction. A pooled full-dataset result conceals operating conditions in which a different method becomes preferable.

5. Do category and style affect the comparison?

  • abstraction surrealism: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.
  • architecture structured: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.
  • high texture brushwork: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.
  • landscape natural: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.
  • portrait figure: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.
Category conclusion. The controlled categories produce different family-balanced outcomes, while fine-grained style results remain less secure where only a small number of independent paintings are available.

6. Synthetic degradations and restoration behaviour

  • dirt dust: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.
  • not applicable: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.
  • partial transparency: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.
  • water stain: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.
  • water stain dirt: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.
  • mild: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.
  • moderate: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.
  • not applicable: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.
  • severe: LaMa is the family-balanced majority outcome.
Synthetic-degradation conclusion. Degradation mechanism changes model behaviour. Water staining, dirt, partial transparency, and combined degradation should not be treated as interchangeable missing-region problems.

7. Where do the metrics disagree?

  • 63 of 79 scope groups contain more than one unique family winner.
  • A family-balanced majority is a compact diagnostic, not a trustworthiness score.
  • Semantic or feature agreement can coexist with colour, texture, or seam failure.
  • Disagreement identifies cases requiring explanation rather than cases that should be discarded.
Disagreement conclusion. Metric disagreement is scientifically useful evidence. Removing it would make the comparison simpler but less trustworthy.

8. Does uncertainty identify speculative behaviour?

  • High seed variability exposes unstable candidate generation.
  • Low seed variability can accompany consistently weak restoration.
  • Uncertainty is model-specific and cannot be assigned retrospectively to deterministic methods or single-seed SDXL.
RQ3 conclusion. Repeated-seed variability identifies some unstable cases, but it does not identify every unreliable restoration and cannot be interpreted as calibrated confidence.

9. Scratch-aware prompt context

  • The scratch-aware prompt improves some paintings and metrics.
  • Other cases regress, so the prompt cannot replace the generic baseline.
  • Prompt changes do not fully solve Stable Diffusion's narrow-mask geometry problem.
  • The ablation remains contextual evidence and is not substituted into the baseline comparison.
Prompt conclusion. Damage-aware language is useful but insufficient. Thin-scratch restoration remains constrained by mask geometry and local continuity, not merely by semantic prompt wording.

  • Telea is the least computationally expensive evaluated method.

Operational conclusion. Deterministic methods support faster broad screening. Generative methods increase both compute cost and the number of outputs requiring human inspection.

12. Thesis-level conclusions

What the evidence supports

  • Painting-restoration evaluation benefits materially from combining classical, perceptual, feature, texture, colour, seam, semantic, spatial, and uncertainty evidence.
  • Model performance is conditional on damage geometry, affected region, degradation mechanism, and painting characteristics.
  • Deterministic methods can outperform generative methods for constrained local repairs.
  • Generative continuation can preserve higher-level content while introducing local inconsistency or unsupported detail.
  • Metric disagreement should be exposed rather than averaged away.
  • Uncertainty identifies some speculative behaviour but requires failure evidence and human review.

What remains unresolved

  • Whether computationally preferred candidates are accepted by professional conservators.
  • Whether learned-feature consistency corresponds to historical plausibility.
  • How these results generalize to naturally deteriorated physical paintings.
  • How later failure flags should be calibrated against human judgements.
  • Whether any generated candidate is suitable for physical conservation intervention.
Contribution to the thesis. Notebook 21 demonstrates a reproducible, museum-oriented evidence structure that makes model strengths, limitations, uncertainty, and metric disagreement visible without equating visual plausibility with authenticity.

13. Extended visual evidence

Open four additional core representative panels

Interpretation limits

  • Reference similarity does not prove historical accuracy.
  • Feature similarity does not prove iconographic correctness.
  • Low pixel error does not prove acceptable brushwork or material compatibility.
  • The 410 cases are nested within 50 paintings.
  • Style metadata is incomplete for part of the dataset.
  • SDXL contains ten cases and one seed per case.
  • Majority voting is not conservation truth.
  • Computational evaluation does not authorize physical intervention.
